Spanish Netherlands
SPAN-ish NETH-er-landz
proper noun (the Low Countries under Spain)
The Low Countries under the rule of Catholic Habsburg Spain in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries; the arena of the Dutch Revolt and the Reformation's costly advance.

Biblical Definition

The Spanish Netherlands were the Low Countries (modern Netherlands and Belgium) under the rule of Catholic Habsburg Spain in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries—the arena of the Dutch Revolt and of the Reformation's costly advance against fierce persecution. As the Reformed faith spread through the provinces, the Spanish crown, under Charles V and Philip II, sought to crush it by the Inquisition, the edicts against heresy, and the sword. The Duke of Alva's “Council of Blood” executed thousands; whole congregations suffered for the gospel; and the resulting revolt, led by William of Orange, eventually won independence for the Protestant northern provinces (the Dutch Republic), while the southern provinces remained Catholic under Spain. Out of this furnace came the Belgic Confession, written by Guido de Brès, himself later martyred, and the Synod of Dort. The dictionary marks the Spanish Netherlands as a solemn theatre of the truth that the church is often born and preserved through blood, and of the providence of God over the rise and fall of nations. The Revelation's vision of the woman drunken with the blood of the saints was read by the Reformed of the persecuting power that slew them; and the Lord's beatitude rested on those persecuted for righteousness' sake. Yet the same God who permitted the persecution restrained and overruled it, for the king's heart is in His hand, and surely the wrath of man shall praise Him, the remainder of wrath He shall restrain. The Spanish Netherlands witness that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church, and that no empire, however mighty, can finally quench the truth God has resolved to preserve.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Low Countries under Catholic Habsburg Spain (16th-17th c.), the arena of the Dutch Revolt and the Reformation's costly advance against persecution; a theatre of martyr-blood and of God's providence over nations, whence came the Belgic Confession and Dort.

SPANISH NETHERLANDS, proper noun. The Low Countries under Catholic Habsburg Spain, 16th-17th centuries.

The arena of the Dutch Revolt and the Reformation's costly advance.

Spain sought to crush the Reformed faith by Inquisition, edict, and the sword.

Alva's “Council of Blood” executed thousands; the revolt won the Protestant north its freedom.

Whence came the Belgic Confession (Guido de Brès) and the Synod of Dort.

Key Scripture

Re 17:6 — "And I saw the woman drunken with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus: and when I saw her, I wondered with great admiration."

Mt 5:10 — "Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven."

Pr 21:1 — "The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will."

Ps 76:10 — "Surely the wrath of man shall praise thee: the remainder of wrath shalt thou restrain."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the secular history that reduces the Dutch Revolt to mere politics, missing the martyr-blood and the providence by which God preserved His church.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the church is often preserved through blood and that God reigns over the nations. Secular history reduces the Dutch Revolt to a tale of taxes, trade, and political independence; the dictionary affirms the political dimension but denies the reduction. At its heart the struggle in the Spanish Netherlands was over the gospel: the Reformed faith spread, Catholic Spain sought to crush it by Inquisition and sword, and thousands suffered for righteousness' sake. The Reformed read in the woman drunken with the blood of the saints the persecuting power that slew them, and the Lord's beatitude rested on the persecuted.

The Spanish Netherlands also display the providence of God over empires. The same God who permitted the persecution restrained and overruled it—the king's heart in His hand, the wrath of man made to praise Him and its remainder restrained. Out of the furnace came the Belgic Confession of the martyr Guido de Brès and the Synod of Dort, enduring fruits of a persecuted church. The dictionary holds the Spanish Netherlands as a witness that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church, and that no empire, however mighty, can finally quench the truth God has resolved to preserve.

Hebrew Roots

The Low Countries (Netherlands and Belgium) under Catholic Habsburg Spain; the theatre of the Dutch Revolt (1568-1648) and of Reformed martyrdom under the Inquisition and the Duke of Alva.

The Low Countries under the rule of Habsburg Spain (Charles V, Philip II).

The Dutch Revolt (1568-1648) led by William of Orange.

The Duke of Alva's “Council of Blood” that executed thousands.

The Protestant north won freedom as the Dutch Republic; the south stayed Catholic.

Whence the Belgic Confession (Guido de Brès) and the Synod of Dort.
